Title: Estimating pros and cons of statistical downscaling based on EQM bias adjustment as a complementary method to dynamical downscaling

The increasing availability of coarse-scale climate simulations and the need for ready-to-use high-
resolution variables drive the climate community to the challenge of reducing computational resources 
and time for downscaling purposes. To this end, statistical downscaling is gaining interest as a 
potential strategy for integrating high-resolution climate information obtained through dynamical 
downscaling over limited years, providing a clear understanding of the gains and losses in combining 
dynamical and statistical downscaling. In this regard, several questions can be raised: (i) what is 
the performance of statistical downscaling, assuming dynamical downscaling as a reference over a 
shared time window; (ii) how much the performance of statistical downscaling is affected by changes 
in the number of years available for training; (iii) how does the climate normal considered for the 
training affect the predictions. This study addresses these issues by applying a statistical downscaling 
procedure based on the empirical quantile mapping bias adjustment, obtaining finer-resolution climate 
variables. This procedure was adopted in order to downscale temperature and precipitation from 
ERA5 climate reanalysis, having as reference both for training and validation, the respective variables 
obtained through the dynamical downscaling of ERA5 over Italy for about 30 years. The availability of 
such a long simulation allows us to define several long time windows, used to calibrate the statistical 
relationships and evaluate the performance of statistical downscaling versus dynamical downscaling 
over a shared blind prediction period, taking advantage of a set of spatial and temporal metrics. The 
study shows that (i) the statistical downscaling successfully represents mean values and extremes 
of temperature and precipitation; (ii) its performance remains satisfactory regardless of the number 
of years used as training; (iii) the shorter is the time window considered for the training, the higher 
is the sensitivity to changes in the time interval due to the inter-annual variability. Nevertheless, the 
performance deviations are somehow not so remarkable.
Keywords  Empirical quantile mapping (EQM), Climate reanalysis, Temperature and precipitation 
downscaling, Performance evaluation, Training period variability
Developing and disseminating reliable climate data is a crucial challenge to downstream climate change analysis 
in several domains, such as promoting climate impact assessment, supporting climate risk management and 
adaptation, and co-designing climate services tailored to users1. In this perspective, coarse-resolution data (e.g., 
climate reanalysis and global climate model, GCM) are relevant for describing past and current climate2,3 and 
assessing the response of the global climate system to increasing greenhouse gas concentrations4,5. However, 
the discrepancy in scale prevents the direct use of this data for regional climate analysis, mainly in areas with 
complex orography or highly heterogeneous land cover, where large-scale models underperform in simulating 
fine-scale (i.e., sub-grid) processes. As a result, dynamical downscaling (DD) and statistical downscaling (SD) 
methods are widely adopted to obtain high-resolution climate information from large-scale models.
DD uses a regional climate model (RCM) forced by reanalysis data or GCM outputs to derive high-resolution 
climate information on a limited area of interest6. SD refers to those methods which identify data-driven

and apply these links during an extrapolation period to derive localised climate model outputs1,7–9. The main 
advantages of SD over DD are its computational efficiency and applicability to several data sources, which may 
not be statistically linked to each other at first glance. Moreover, SD may be used with a lower availability of 
observational data since the algorithms can find significant statistical relationships between large-scale and 
local/regional variables. Nevertheless, by construction, SD relies on historical statistical relationships, and 
therefore, it may underestimate or miss future events that were never observed in the past. In a changing climate, 
this assumption leads to uncertainties within SD methods, supporting the DD approaches. Nevertheless, the 
latter need high computational costs and are then quite expensive. High-resolution RCMs nested within GCMs 
are used to determine the physical processes through physical equations and mathematical parametrisations. 
By construction, DD may provide a detailed representation of regional processes at high resolution and more 
accurate projections at local scales. Nevertheless, it is worth mentioning that it is susceptible to the model choices 
and hence, an ensemble of climate models is always recommended to evaluate model uncertainties. Moreover, a 
bias correction step is generally applied to reduce uncertainties in climate models.
Many studies compared the performance of SD and DD, showing how the use of one method instead of 
another may lead to differences in the simulated variables10–13. In this respect, Ayar et al.11 compared SD and DD 
methods over the European domain, showing that SD methods better simulate the occurrence and intensity of 
rain, whereas RCMs better simulate spatial variability and temporal precipitation variability. Some studies, such 
as Su et al.14, showed that the two downscaling methods reasonably reproduce the spatial pattern and monthly 
rainfall in the rainy season over the Heihe River basin in China, while others, such as Attique et al.15, reported 
that SD better than DD simulate rainfall over the Gwadar-Ormara basin in Pakistan.
Several SD methods have been developed through the years16, including physical scaling17,18, bias-correction 
spatial downscaling19–22, stepwise clustered downscaling23,24, and artificial neural networks25–29. In this context, 
the EU COST Action VALUE initiative30 conducted an in-depth evaluation of statistical downscaling methods 
applied to climate modelling through three key experiments: the first tested the performance of different 
statistical downscaling methods in the current climate, using perfect predictors (i.e., observations or reanalysis 
data); the second examined the overall effectiveness of these methods when driven by predictors from GCMs; 
the third focused on evaluating downscaling skills in future climate scenarios, simulating a pseudo-future 
environment. The main results indicated that bias correction methods generally perform better, but they rely on 
high-quality predictors with a resolution close to the target. In contrast, perfect prognosis methods are highly 
dependent on the choice of predictors and model structure, often facing difficulties in representing interannual 
and spatial variability, solved by using RCMs.
Nowadays, the availability of high-density local weather stations and high-level satellite information and 
the increase in computing performance makes it possible to produce high-resolution gridded observations31–33 
and run convection-permitting (CP-) RCMs with kilometre-scale grids (i.e. < 4 km). However, these products 
still feature low temporal coverage (e.g., 10–20 years), except in a few cases34–37. CP-RCMs are gaining broad 
attention from the climate community as promising tools to identify surface heterogeneities and improve the 
representation of atmospheric patterns38,39.
On this topic, Ban et al.40 and Pichelli et al.41 analysed the first 10-years multi-model CP-RCMs ensembles 
for the greater Alpine region, driven by ERA-Interim reanalysis42 and CMIP5-GCMs43, respectively. Moreover, 
Kendon et al.34 produced a multi-model ensemble (12 members) of climate projections over the United Kingdom 
at 2.2 km for three 20-year periods (1981–2000, 2021–2040 and 2061–2080) under the CMIP5-RCP8.5 scenario. 
Finally, Reder et al.36 presented ERA5@2km, a high-resolution dataset for 20 European cities, which provides 
input data for pluvial flooding risk analysis44.
Focusing on Italy, Raffa et al.35 recently released VHR-REA_IT (Very High-Resolution REAnalysis for ITaly), 
an hourly gridded simulation for the recent past thirty years (1989–2020) over Italy, obtained by dynamically 
downscaling ERA5 reanalysis45 from its native resolution (≃31 km) to a resolution of ≃ 2.2 km. Furthermore, 
Adinolfi et al.46 widely evaluated the capability of VHR-REA_IT simulation to realistically represent the 
climatology for 2  m temperature and precipitation over the whole peninsula and specific subdomains, 
focusing on hourly precipitation patterns, orography effects, and urban climate dynamics. While, Giordani 
et al.47 presented SPHERA (High-resolution Reanalysis over Italy), a convection-permitting reanalysis over 
Italy, with a resolution of 2.2 km spanning the years 1995–2020. SPHERA was generated through dynamic 
downscaling of ERA5, employing a nudging data assimilation technique to align the model with observational 
data. Moreover, Capecchi et al.48 introduced a weather hindcast at a convection-permitting scale obtained by 
dynamically downscaling ERA5 over Italy for 1979–2019 using two limited-area models (i.e., BOLAM with grid 
spacing = 7 km over the Mediterranean domain and MOLOCH with grid spacing = 2.5 km over Italy) nested 
within each other. Finally, Raffa et al.37 delivered VHR-PRO_IT (Very High-Resolution PROjections for ITaly), a 
60-year climate projection (i.e., 1989–2050) over Italy carried out by dynamically downscaling the Italy8km-CM 
climate projection49 to the same spatial (≃2.2 km) and temporal (hourly) resolution of VHR-REA_IT under the 
CMIP5-RCP4.5 and -RCP8.5 scenarios.
Although cutting-edge works, producing this data required a considerable effort in computing resources and 
time. This effort could potentially represent a limitation in a community where GCM simulations are rapidly 
increasing in availability and need to be incorporated into downscaled climate data products for application in 
regional climate change impacts and adaptation initiatives21. The question arises whether SD can be a viable 
strategy to complement the high-resolution information obtained through DD over limited years, as long as 
there is a clear understanding of the advantages and disadvantages of combining DD and SD50,51. Assessing these 
pros and cons is quite useful for the climate community and therefore, within this work, they are investigated. 
Specifically, the study attempts to address the following questions:

The novelty of this work lies not in the methodology adopted for the downscaling, which is commonly used 
in literature, but in the evaluation of the ability of SD approaches to possibly complement very-high spatial 
resolution (i.e., the CP-RCM one) dynamical downscaling models, when they cover short time periods. To assess 
this aspect is relevant given the increasing availability of CP-RCMs.
The paper first describes (§ 2) the SD workflow (§ 2.1) with a focus on the Empirical Quantile Mapping 
(EQM) bias adjustment approach (§ 2.2), showing the strategy adopted to address the three scientific questions 
mentioned above (§ 2.3) and the spatial and temporal metrics selected to assess model performance in prediction, 
taking VHR-REA_IT as the reference (§ 2.4). Then, it presents the results (§ 3) obtained to address the three 
scientific questions (§ 3.1, § 3.3, § 3.4) and compare the EQM-SD to the PS-SD (§ 3.2). Finally, it discusses and 
summarises their pros and cons (§ 4) to highlight the need to have a complementary use of SD and DD.
Data and methods
SD workflow
Figure 1 shows the workflow proposed here to statistically downscale a climate variable from a coarse to a finer 
grid.
Firstly, a correspondence between coarse and fine grids is established by mapping the values of the climate 
variable of the native to the reference resolution using the nearest-neighbour (NN) interpolation method. 
Subsequently, point-by-point quantile matching is set between the raw interpolated and reference time series 
during the training phase using the Empirical Quantile Mapping (EQM) method52–54. This matching is intended 
to statistically align the interpolated cumulative distribution function (CDF) with that of the reference data. It 
is important to highlight that point-by-point quantile matching is computed on a monthly basis to preserve the 
seasonal patterns and temporal sequences of climate data. Finally, the same correlations derived during training 
are applied to derive high-resolution climate variables for the prediction period.
In this study, the workflow of Fig. 1 has been implemented to statistically downscale daily temperature and 
precipitation of ERA5 to match the spatial resolution of VHR-REA_IT, for which ERA5 is the parent simulation.
In brief:
•	 ERA545 is the fifth generation of reanalysis released by the ECMWF, representing the most plausible descrip­
tion of the current climate. It has global coverage with a spatial resolution of 0.25◦ (≃ 31 km) and provides 
outputs at an hourly frequency from 1950 to today. It was obtained using a 10-members ensemble of 4D var­
iational data assimilation method, favouring uncertainty estimation for each variable.
•	 VHR-REA_IT35 is a climate simulation over Italy obtained by dynamically downscaling ERA5 from its na­
tive resolution to ≃ 2.2 km using the RCM COSMO-CLM. It constitutes a detailed dataset of climatological 
data for about 30 years (i.e., 1989–2020) at the convection-permitting scale. Nowadays, this dataset provides 
high-quality historical climate data, allowing the investigation of processes from regional down to local scale.

Furthermore, the outcomes of the NN-EQM-SD method are assessed against those obtained using both simply 
interpolating ERA5 onto the finer grid with NN method (i.e., NN-SD) and a further SD technique, specifically 
the Physical Scaling (PS) method55–57. In brief, the PS-SD method refines coarse climate data to local scales by 
adjusting for factors like orography. For temperature, it uses a lapse rate to account for elevation changes, while 
for precipitation, it applies a scaling factor based on differences between coarse and fine-resolution models. 
This process involves interpolating data to a finer grid and then reintroducing localized effects to achieve more 
accurate, location-specific climate data (for more details, see Supplementary Material 1). We investigated the 
PS-SD method independently and in conjunction with additional post-processing via the EQM. The aim is to 
assess the differences between the different SD methods (i.e., NN-SD, NN-EQM-SD and PS-SD) and the effect of 
the first step illustrated in Fig. 1, which involves interpolation (matching with nearest-neighbour vs. physically-
based interpolation).
Bias adjustment approach: empirical quantile mapping (EQM)
Bias adjustment methods are commonly adopted to partially remove the systematic biases of global and regional 
model outputs using a specific gridded or point-scale reference. Various methods with differing levels of 
complexity exist for this purpose. They range from simple techniques calibrating the mean to those that adjust all 
quantiles, either parametric or empirical, trend-preserving or not, and with different treatments of new extremes 
and the wet-day frequency for precipitation9,58,59. Applying a bias adjustment method rather than another 
introduces a significant source of uncertainty. In literature, it is generally recommended to use multiple bias 
adjustment techniques, such as the standard empirical and parametric quantile mapping and trend-preserving 
methods7,9,60. In this regard, Casanueva et al.9, investigating the impact of eight bias adjustment methods 
over the Iberian Peninsula on the temperature and precipitation fields, suggested using trend-preserving 
methods. These methods were found to reduce biases while conserving the raw climate change signal, making 
them particularly suitable for applications involving long time-series. As the aim of this study is to assess the 
performance of the SD against DD on short time windows (not including climate scenarios), the bias adjustment 
method adopted (see Fig. 1) is the non-parametric empirical quantile mapping (EQM)52,53,64. However, in future 
studies, this approach could be broadened to encompass other bias-adjustment techniques, thereby exploring 
the performance of SD against DD over a longer time-series.
The EQM is recognised as one of the most used methods in the literature. In brief, it involves training transfer 
functions over a control period, mapping all the quantiles from the empirical CDF of model outputs onto the 
corresponding reference distribution. When adopted in a non-parametric manner, this method offers significant 
flexibility, as it eliminates the need to choose specific statistical functions to fit empirical CDFs. This flexibility 
allows EQM to be applicable to any climate variable, regardless of the statistical function that might better 
represent it, as long as a distribution can be estimated. This includes managing seasonality and accounting for 
non-rainy days, as explained later.

Operatively, EQM first estimates the reference’s and model’s CDFs from daily data over a set of regularly spaced 
quantile levels, using linear interpolation to obtain values between the quantiles. Additionally, it incorporates a 
constant extrapolation (first and last corrections for values below and above the calibration range, respectively) 
to handle out-of-sample values. Then, this empirical correction function h is applied to the projection data, 
yielding projected bias-adjusted model data. Notably, this correction function h is calibrated on a monthly basis 
to preserve the seasonality of the reference climate. It is important to highlight that, for precipitation, EQM 
adjusts wet-day occurrences using a threshold (1 mm/day) which matches the reference and model wet/dry day 
frequency. Finally, it implements a frequency adaptation method61 to simulate precipitation where the model 
overestimates the number of dry days.
Even if EQM is widely used in literature, it has some limitations: (i) the function h is assumed to remain 
constant during prediction without considering specific corrections for trends or allowing for modifications if 
biases are intensity-dependent7,62; (ii) the simulated variables may still retain biases even after the correction 
due to the sensitivity of the method to outliers63; (iii) there may be potential physical inconsistencies, both 
spatially and temporally, between variables when they are bias-corrected independently64. Moreover, additional 
limitations may arise when EQM is used to downscale precipitation, including misrepresentations of the spatial 
and temporal structure, overcorrection of the drizzle effect, and an overestimation of extreme events, as well as 
distortion in precipitation trends65.
However, previous studies investigated the impact of bias correction techniques on modifying the RCM 
projections to address these issues. For instance, Dosio and Paruolo19 showed how successfully implementing 
EQM might enhance RCM precipitation and temperature projections. Indeed, EQM may improve the statistics 
of the simulated results, which are strongly dependent on the evolution of the original fields, such as the number 
of consecutive dry days and the total amount of precipitation following heavy precipitation events. At the same 
time, it may also improve the CDFs of the simulated precipitation and temperature variables.
Selection of training and validation periods
The selection of training and validation periods relied on the need to address the three scientific questions 
outlined in the Introduction (§  1). Regarding the first scientific question, we divided the analysis into two 
distinct periods: the first spanning 20 years (1989–2008) dedicated to training the quantile matching, and the 
latter spanning the remaining 12 years (2009–2020) designated as the blind prediction period to evaluate the 
predictive performance of the SD procedure. This experimental setup is denoted as CASE A (see Supplementary 
Material 2, Fig. SM1).
After analysing the prediction performance of NN-EQM-SD, the second scientific question in this study is 
to quantify the sensitivity of NN-EQM-SD skills to the number of years available for training. To address this, 
we designed a further experiment, CASE B (see Supplementary Material 2, Fig. SM1), which employs a training 
time window of 10 years (1989–1998) while sharing the same validation period (2009–2020) as CASE A. This 
configuration facilitates a comparative analysis of the outcomes between the two experiments, with VHR-REA_
IT as the reference.
The last scientific question aims to understand the sensitivity of the NN-EQM-SD method to the time 
window chosen as the calibration period, keeping the width of the time window constant (10 years). To this 
aim, a sensitivity was performed by moving the training window forward in time, with a 1-year step, from 1989 
to 1998 (corresponding to CASE B) to 1998–2008 (see Supplementary Material 2, Fig. SM2), obtaining thus 
11 potential combinations. The sensitivity was completed by analysing additional 20 potential combinations, 
randomly selecting 10 years within the period 1989–2008 (see Supplementary Material 2, Fig. SM3) to reduce 
potential trends and characterize internal variability.
The decision to adopt a moving window approach (10-year time windows) instead of entirely random 
sampling aligns with the aim of complementing SD with existing DD experiments, which typically span 
continuous periods of similar durations40,41.

These metrics encompass straightforward statistical parameters commonly adopted to quantify the model skills, 
as well as more intricate diagnostics. In this study, they have been categorised into metrics adopted for spatial 
performance analysis, e.g., through map comparisons and metrics used to investigate performance in terms of 
temporal evolution via time-series comparisons.

•	 POD describes the fraction of reference events correctly predicted (range in-between 0, i.e., not even one

In practice, a map of annual average values over a certain number of years (referred to as the reference map) is 
considered for a dataset like VHR-REA_IT, and a specific threshold is determined (e.g., the 50th percentile of 
the data). This is then compared to a corresponding map for the same period (referred to as the derived map), 
which may be produced using methods such as NN-EQM-SD. For each grid point ij, if both the reference and 
derived values exceed the threshold, a value of Aij=1 is assigned. If both values are below the threshold, Dij=1 
is assigned. If the reference value is above the threshold while the derived value is below it, Bij=1 is assigned, 
indicating a missed prediction. Conversely, if the reference value is below the threshold and the derived value 
exceeds it, Cij=1 is assigned, indicating a false prediction. The final values (A, B, C, D) are obtained by summing 
all ij values and dividing by the total number of grid points.
From a graphical viewpoint, the performance diagram shows SR on the x-axis and POD on the y-axis. CSI 
and bias are contour lines depending on a combination in-between POD and SR. The best performance is related 
to the upper right corner of the diagram (POD, SR, CSI and frequency bias approach unity) and along the 
diagonal where the frequency bias is 1. Deviations in a particular direction indicate relative differences in POD 
and SR and, thus, in frequency bias and CSI.

Results
Performance of EQM-SD against DD
The first Section compares the performance of the NN-EQM-SD against the DD for the temperature and 
precipitation fields using the experiment configuration referred to CASE A (see Supplementary Material 2, 
Fig. SM1). As support, the intermediate result obtained by simply interpolating ERA5 onto the VHR-REA_IT 
grid using the nearest-neighbour method (i.e., NN-SD) is also reported to highlight the role of using EQM. 
Temperature and precipitation have been evaluated in blind prediction by computing specific features such as 
the temporal mean value and statistics for extremes (i.e., 1st and 99th percentile of temperature time series 
over the blind prediction period and 99th percentile of daily precipitation time series over the blind prediction 
period) for each land grid point. Notably, the 99th percentile of precipitation has been computed by including 
values below 1 mm/day following Schär et al.69. Moreover, the spatial distributions of mean temperature and 
mean daily precipitation have been investigated at seasonal scale (i.e., DJF: December-January-February; MAM: 
March-April-May; JJA: June-July-August; SON: September-October-November). Finally, in addition to this 
spatial investigation, the monthly evolution of the mean values in blind prediction has been analysed by spatially 
averaging over the analysis domain.
Spatial and temporal metrics have been exploited to assess NN-SD and NN-EQM-SD performances 
objectively. Specifically, MAE and NRMSE are used for spatial model evaluation, and KGE is used for temporal 
model evaluation. The spatial metrics are calculated on the various maps shown in the following figures with data 
temporally aggregated. In contrast, the KGE is computed by spatially aggregating the monthly data, resulting in 
an average time series that represents the evaluation domain.
Temperature
Figure 3 shows the spatial distribution of the temporal mean (Fig. 3a) of the temperature returned by VHR-
REA_IT over Italy for 2009–2020. Spatially, the values are consistent with the orography of the study area, with 
values decreasing as altitude increases. In particular, the mean temperature (Fig. 3a) has values between 4 °C and 
18 °C (5th and 95th percentile of the spatial distribution). Comparing NN-SD with VHR-REA_IT (see Fig. 3b), 
a significant divergence between the interpolated data and the reference data is noticeable. In particular, the 
visual inspection of the bias in the spatial distribution of the temporal mean shows a tendency for NN-SD to be 
warmer in areas with higher elevation and cooler in flatter areas. This behaviour at higher elevations is linked to 
the differences in orography reported in Fig. 2. The spatial metrics (see Table 1) confirm this strong divergence

Discussion and conclusion
This work investigated if SD can be a valid strategy for integrating high-resolution climate data from DD over 
limited years. To do this, ERA5 was statistically downscaled to the same spatial resolution as VHR-REA_IT, of 
which ERA5 is the parent simulation, using the EQM as the SD tool. Specifically, it addressed the three objectives 
claimed in the Introduction as follows:
	 i.	 The NN-EQM-SD was able to satisfactorily, both spatially and temporally, derive the temperature and pre­
cipitation values (and their extremes) in blind prediction w.r.t. DD. In particular, as expected, better perfor­
mance is gained by the temperature field compared to the precipitation, whose frequencies of wet/dry days 
also affect the bias adjustment. Moreover, the pre-processing interpolation step plays a minor role compared 
with the bias adjustment, as proved by comparing the results from PS-EQM-SD against NN-EQM-SD.
	ii.	 The performance of SD for temperature and precipitation in prediction remains satisfactory, even changing 
the number of years available for the model training (10; 20 years). This aspect was analysed using perfor­
mance diagrams for mean and extreme characteristics at different threshold values. This result is of consid­
erable importance as a growing number of experiments at very high resolution but with limited temporal 
extension are available, which could be completed to some extent by statistical methods.
	iii.	 The time span considered for the training of the statistical method has its relevance as, for a short time 
width (10-year), it could be affected by internal variability. Nevertheless, even if this aspect undermines the 
credibility of a possible complement of limited years of analysis with DD using statistical methods, it has 
been shown, on the other hand, that the performance deviations are somehow irrelevant. This insight could 
settle the basis for a compromise between the dynamic and statistical approach and support the definition 
of more efficient downscaling strategies to be employed. Indeed, if it is true that DD is physically based and 
also more credible, it is also true that it requires considerably longer calculation time. As a rough estima­

Although the achieved performances are already promising, several limitations and sources of uncertainty of 
the EQM-SD must be carefully considered to get a more credible framework. Firstly, the temporal length of the 
data sample was used to train the point-by-point statistical relationships. In this respect, it is widely recognized 
in the literature that to statistically train a model, the calibration period should be at least 30 years long to reduce 
the effect of internal climate variability. Nevertheless, this work considered periods of 20-year to address the 
question (i) and 10-year for questions (ii) and (iii) to cope with the need to split the reference DD product (i.e., 
VHR-REA_IT, covering 32-year) both in the training and the benchmark to validate the prediction over a shared 
blind prediction period. The comparison between EQM-SD and DD demonstrated somewhat contamination of 
the findings due to this mismatch as noticeable by an internal trend when the 10-year training window moves 
forward by one year. Although this internal trend would discourage the use of a 10-year time window for training, 
it was important to quantify the loss that would be incurred compared to the use of longer training windows 
(e.g. 20 years, see Fig. 14) as cutting-edge very high-resolution climate data are usually available for limited 
time windows, setting us in a “real world scenario”. Moreover, it is essential to estimate possible reductions 
in performance if statistical techniques (NN-EQM-SD or other SD techniques) are used to extend data time-
series. This limitation may be overcome if datasets obtained with high-resolution DD techniques are available 
for extended periods.
The second limitation refers to the bias adjustment method adopted in this work (i.e., EQM) and especially 
to the assumption of stationarity based on it. Casanueva et al.9 compared different bias correction methods, 
proving they represent a significant source of uncertainty. Indeed, most methods should potentially modify the 
climate signal from the raw model output when data are bias-adjusted. In this sense, EQM is one of the methods 
that can generate this situation, neglecting any specific corrections for trends. Nevertheless, such changes 
might be advantageous in some cases. For example, some authors72,73 stated that the bias adjustment improves 
the climate change signal by removing the intensity-dependent errors in the original models that cause this 
alteration. On the same issue, Dosio54 claimed that a climate signal alteration might be justified for highly biased 
climate indices such as those defined using absolute thresholds, where the raw signal could be unreliable. Other 
authors52,53,59 suggested that it is preferable to adopt approaches that explicitly preserve relative changes between 
bias-adjusted and non-bias-adjusted climate projections, especially as fundamental errors in the climate model 
cannot be resolved by statistical post-processing7.
Furthermore, they explained that trend-preserving methods are desirable if there are no physical mechanisms 
to justify a change and the model returns a credible climate change signal. This dispute has a minor implication 
in this work, as only a few years of data have been considered, and the climate signal has just been ignored. 
However, it is one of the points to be analysed for future work developments whenever the same workflow is 
supposed to be employed for a much longer time series. In this sense, a good practice would be to build an 
ensemble of bias correction methods to measure the spread of the obtained projections data, considering other 
QM-based techniques (e.g., nested bias-correction by Johnson and Sharma74).
The third and last limitation and source of uncertainty to keep in mind are precisely related to the use 
of bias-correction spatial downscaling as an SD technique. In general, several shortcomings affect SD based 
on bias correction. Indeed, the high-resolution reference signal may induce statistical artefacts and a wrong 
representation of spatiotemporal structures to explain unexplained smaller-scale variability7. Two primary 
sources of uncertainty affecting SD based on bias correction are (a) observational uncertainty and (b) spatial 
resolution mismatch between model outputs and observations9. In this work, the first source of uncertainty is 
partly coped with using a model climate data as a reference, thus limiting errors and uncertainties typical of 
local observations (e.g., different spatial density of measurement points and eventual presence of data gaps). 
Conversely, the second source of uncertainty is neglected, as the resolution mismatch has not been adequately 
investigated, considering a direct jump from 31 to 2.2 km. To this end, future work could be aimed at analysing 
and evaluating the EQM-SD performance for different resolution jumps. Moreover, it is recognized that the 
resolution mismatch typically requires applying more general SD techniques, such as regression, analog-
based and artificial neural networks27,75. Finally, as future developments, the SD method should be tested for 
downscaling long-term climate projections (e.g. CMIP6), incorporating variables at higher temporal resolutions 
(e.g., sub-daily to hourly) and accounting for location-specific and temporal biases. Additionally, the influence 
of long-term internal variability, challenges related to cross-validation in the presence of such variability, and 
the broader question of how to effectively evaluate bias adjustment in a realistic setting—i.e., when using 
long-term climate projections where the EQM-SD method may often fall outside the training range—should 
be carefully considered. Indeed, the use of a highly idealised “perfect” predictor setup, with ERA5 as input 
and a high-resolution reanalysis (i.e., VHR-REA_IT) as reference, provided an advantageous position, which 
obviously needs to be emphasised. Nonetheless, this work could represent a small step forward in supporting 
the development of semi-operational products, enabling the rapid downscaling of reanalyses (not only VHR-
REA_IT, but also other products such as the CERRA reanalysis76 and others), as well as seasonal forecasts, where 
non-stationarity plays a minor role in the short term. In an operational context, this near-real-time localisation 
would provide significant added value to both the climate modelling and impact assessment communities77.
Considering these points, it is essential to recognize that DD models remain highly significant in climate 
studies78. They can simultaneously simulate various surface and atmospheric variables across different levels, 
ensuring physical consistency, even in complex terrain, as well as accurately reproducing coastal processes and 
extreme events (mainly with RCMs at the convection-permitting scale). Additionally, DD can represent local
